events.venue_address: Second Avenue & East Houston Street, New York, NY 10003
events.description:
This holiday season, the New York Transit Museum and MTA New York City Transit continue the annual tradition of Holiday Nostalgia Rides aboard vintage 1930s subway cars. Operating between 2 Av–Houston St on the uptown F line and 96 St–2 Av on the Q line, the Holiday Nostalgia Train will transport straphangers back in time every Sunday between Thanksgiving and New Year’s from 10am to 5pm.
Hop aboard and celebrate the magic of New York City during the holidays — rides are free with your subway fare!
New this year!
Take a closer look as you travel back in time! Our Holiday Nostalgia Ride Scavenger Hunt invites you to spot and photograph vintage details, from rattan seats and ceiling fans to authentic roll signs and Miss Subways ads. Discover what these features reveal about subway travel in the 1930s, and find them all to earn a prize! Download the free
New York Transit Museum App
before your ride to join the fun.

Program Experience
Nostalgia Rides happen rain or shine. Equipment, route, timing, and duration are subject to change. Restrooms are not available on the trains.

Please keep arms, hands and cameras inside the train. Walking between train cars is not allowed.
The first car of the train is a magical place for everyone. Please consider our youngest visitors and allow children to look out the front window.
Help us preserve these vintage cars for future generations!

Learn about Grand Central’s long history of expansion, culminating in its most recent addition, Grand Central Madison, on this walking tour. events.venue_name: Penn Station / Moynihan Train Hall (approximate meeting point; check ticket instructions)
events.description:
Members enjoy early access! Tickets go on sale to Museum members on Wednesday, August 5 at 10am ET. Remaining tickets go on sale to the public Friday, August 7 at 10am ET.
Explore the rich history of New York City, past and present, one neighborhood at a time. Through the lens of transportation, discover new places, share stories, and connect with communities.
Penn Station, a Beaux-Arts masterpiece with grand columns and Roman-inspired design, forged a vital gateway to New York City from the west when it debuted in 1910. 50 years later, a decline in rail travel, the rise of the automobile, and lucrative real estate interests led to the station’s demolition, sparking a controversy that helped ignite the city’s historic preservation movement. Today, the station’s transit footprint has expanded to Moynihan Train Hall, and touches of its past grandeur have been reintroduced through new public artworks.
Discover hidden architectural remnants and artwork throughout this transportation hub and explore its ongoing transformation on this walking tour.

events.title: MTA Open Data for System Improvements
events.description:
What happens at a station when it is closed for service? Keeping a 24/7 transit system running safely and reliably requires complex maintenance and upgrades that inevitably impact riders. To increase efficiency and reduce this impact, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) uses data to bundle work orders and plan customer communications, much of which is publicly available through MTA’s Open Data Program.
Join Senior Director Enterprise Asset Management Value Realization, Kayla Sadallah, Assistant Vice President, Stations Quality Assurance and Ops Support, Samuel Wong, and Director of Data Science, MTA Data and Analytics, Ryan Mulvey, as they break down the process behind planning, executing, and communicating work orders, and explore how data increasingly helps teams streamline these efforts.

events.description:
Community Arts Grantee:
The Tallichet Foundation
Date:
Exhibition on View: November 2 - November 15, 2026
Panel Talk and Special Performance: November 14, 2026
Location:
Lorimoto Gallery
1623 Hancock St, Queens, NY 11385
Event Description:
The Tallichet Freedman Foundation is pleased to present Stone’s Throw, an exhibition of twenty
visual artists from our first two micro grant cycles, hosted by Lorimoto Gallery in Ridgewood,
Queens. The exhibition will take place from
November 2 through November 15, 2026
, and will be
open Tuesday through Sunday, 12:00 to 6:00 PM.
Stone’s Throw includes work from the artists Lillian Ansell, Steven Bukowski, Nickolas Calabrese,
Marilla Cubberley, Hillary Gabryel, Kyra Gregory, Apolline Guillerot-Malick, Anne Hart, Amelia
Heintzelman, Michelle Im, Maite Iribarren Vázquez, Emily Janowick, Monte Marin, Devin Osorio,
TJ Proechel, Andrew Ross, Maíra Senise, Jeanette Spicer, Alina Tenser, and Sarah Trigg.
At the time of their grant awards, all twenty artists lived or worked in the 11385 ZIP code of
Queens, NY, and most continue to do so today. Together, their work offers a creative portrait of
our vibrant neighborhood, showcasing sculpture, drawing, painting, photography, performance,
and design. TTFF is proud to present the artists’ work to the public.
A panel discussion and performance with the artists will take place Saturday, November 14th at
6:30 PM, hosted by writer, curator, and educator Sara Nadal-Melsió.
About The Tallichet Foundation:
The Tallichet Freedman Foundation (TTFF) supports visual artists in Ridgewood, Queens through
unrestricted micro grants, filmed studio interviews, gatherings, exhibitions, and public
programming. We create opportunities for artists across generations, backgrounds, and stages
of their careers, particularly those outside traditional art world structures, to connect, share
ideas, and build relationships. TTFF is intentionally hyper-local, investing in artists where they
live and work.
Learn more about the Tillichet Foundation.

Join us at
Lewis Latimer House
for the next installment of
Mapping Queens
, a conversation series presented as part of Flushing Town Hall's
Queens Cultural Mapping Initiative
, highlighting the people and organizations shaping Queens' cultural landscape.
Moderated by
Natalie Bedon
, Project Manager of the Queens Cultural Mapping Initiative, this conversation will feature cultural leaders preserving and reimagining historic houses and heritage sites across Queens:
Carl Ballenas — Friends of Maple Grove Cemetery
Debby Silverfine — Voelker Orth Museum
Kelsey Brow — King Manor Museum
Ran Yan — Lewis Latimer House
Panelists will explore how historic sites preserve Queens' diverse histories while serving as vibrant spaces for arts, education, and community engagement. About Lewis Latimer House
Lewis Latimer House is a historic house museum in Flushing dedicated to preserving the legacy of Lewis Howard Latimer, a pioneering African American inventor, engineer, and artist. Through exhibitions, STEAM education, and public programming, the museum connects Latimer's contributions to broader conversations about innovation, creativity, and social justice.

This December, step into a dream where mariachi trumpets meet Tchaikovsky’s strings, Aztec-inspired dance and ballet share the same stage, and a young girl discovers what it means to belong to two cultures at once.

follows a Mexican American girl growing up in New York City, torn between the traditions her immigrant parents hold sacred and the American holiday magic all around her. From the sacred dances honoring La Virgen de Guadalupe to the glittering wonder of

Calpulli Mexican Dance Company (hereafter “Calpulli”) is a professional touring company celebrating Mexican and Mexican American culture through dance and music. Based in New York City, the company produces performances that tell folk stories of Mexico’s diverse ethnic and historical influences.

events.description:
This immersive 6-hour workshop introduces students to the art of canister Damascus steel.
Canister Damascus is a distinctive form of pattern-welded steel created by forging a mixture of powdered steel and solid metal pieces inside a sealed steel container, or "canister." Under intense heat and pressure, these materials fuse into a single solid billet. Once the canister is removed, the billet reveals unique, often unpredictable patterns that make every piece one of a kind.
In this hands-on class, students will design and assemble a canister billet, forge-weld it, and draw it out using our induction forge in Brooklyn. The course covers safety, material selection, canister preparation, forge welding, and basic forging techniques. By the end of the class, each student will leave with a forged Damascus billet ready for further refinement.
Students are encouraged to bring clean steel items to include in their billets, such as springs or ball bearings. Materials must be free of grease, oil, paint, and other contaminants. Contact us if you have questions about suitable materials.

events.title: The 1778 Treaty with the Delaware: A Roundtable
events.description:
BPL Presents welcomes the Lenape Center’s Joe Baker and Hadrien Coumans back to the stage, along with Pace University Law Professor Nicholas A. Robinson—to discuss the treaties of the Lenape with the United States. Co-presented with the Lenape Center, this conversation will be moderated by Joseph T. Murphy of Humanities New York.
Building on a partnership begun with the 2022 Lenapehoking Exhibition and the resulting
Lenapehoking Anthology
, this unique conversation will explore how the treaties respected the sovereignty of the Delaware Tribe, also known as the Lenape, from the 17th century to 1863. Beginning with colonial treaties, the Lenape have the longest record of treaties and the largest number of treaties of any Tribe. Why have they been forgotten? The United States claims the 1778 Treaty with the Delaware, agreed during the Revolutionary War, to be the first US treaty with any Indian Nation.
Following the Treaty with France earlier that year, this Treaty is only the second treaty the USA had ever negotiated with any other nation. Deemed essential to winning the American War of Independence 250 years ago, the Continental Congress sought an alliance with the Delaware, and as allies both made promises. The U.S. pledged to consider inviting the Delaware to gather tribes to become a 14th state, together with the confederation of the 13 states seeking their independence from Britain. What would the young United States be like if the agreed terms in this treaty had prevailed? What do subsequent treaties tell us about the relationship of the Lenape and the USA?
PARTICIPANTS
Hadrien Coumans
is co-founder and Deputy Director of Lenape Center in New York and a traditionally adopted member of the Lenape WhiteTurkey–Fugate family. For 27 years, he has worked alongside Lenape elder Joe Baker, guided by a shared charge of cultural and institutional responsibility. For nearly twenty years, Lenape Center has restored Lenape presence, history, and knowledge in New York City through the arts, culture, education, and institutional partnerships. It also brings Lenape peacemaking principles to institutional culture, public narrative, and policy. Coumans holds United States Institute of Peace certifications in Conflict Analysis, Mediating Violent Conflict, and Land, Property & Conflict, and has trained in Trauma Awareness and Resilience. He has spoken at the United Nations, Brooklyn Law School, Pace School of Law, and Cardozo Law School’s Ferencz Human Rights & Atrocity Prevention Clinic. He has also addressed the governments of Australia, Finland, the Netherlands, and Canada. A writer and editor as well, he is co-editor of Lenapehoking: An Anthology, co-published by Lenape Center and Brooklyn Public Library. He has served as Associate Faculty at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health. His writing includes “Wëlamàlsewakàn: Reimagining the Right to Health through Lenape Epistemologies” in Harvard’s Health and Human Rights Journal.
Joe Baker
(Lenape, Delaware Tribe of Indians) is an artist, educator, curator, and Vietnam Era U.S. Air Force veteran. He served with the 308th Strategic Missile Wing, which oversaw Titan II intercontinental ballistic missiles. He has worked in Native arts for forty years. He is a descendant of Lenape leaders who took part in treaty diplomacy, including Captain Anderson Sarcoxie, Captain White Eyes, Netawatwees, and Tamanend. Baker is co-founder and executive director of the Lenape Center in Manhattan. For nearly twenty years, the Center has restored Lenape presence, history, and knowledge in New York City through the arts, culture, education, and institutional partnerships. It also brings Lenape peacemaking principles to institutional culture, public narrative, and policy.  Under Baker’s direction, the Center has partnered with the Metropolitan Museum of Art  and taken part in Cooper Hewitt’s Making Home. It co-published Lenapehoking: An Anthology with Brooklyn Public Library. Baker curated Lenapehoking, the first Lenape-curated exhibition of Lenape cultural arts in New York City, at Brooklyn Public Library. Baker holds a BFA and an MFA from the University of Tulsa. He completed postgraduate study at Harvard’s Graduate School of Education and is Visiting Professor of Museum Studies at Colorado College.
Nicholas A. Robinson
is the Gilbert & Sarah Kerlin Distinguished Professor of Environmental Law
Emeritus
in the Elisabeth Haub School of Law at Pace University based in White Plains, New York. He has taught environmental law since 1978 at Haub Law School and lectured widely abroad on comparative and international environmental law, including the customary  law of Indigenous Peoples. He chaired the Commission on Environmental Law of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN). At the invitation of the Lenape Center, he led a research seminar at Haub Law School studying the treaties of the Lenape Nation, beginning with  the treaty of Shackamaxon, negotiated by Tamanend for the Delaware and William Penn for the English (1682), through to US Continental Congress’ Treaty of 1778 with the Delaware and the treaties of the 19
th
century. His published scholarship includes the first history of the Forest Charter (
carta de foresta
) of 1217, and range of works on comparative and international law.
Joseph T. Murphy
is Director of Strategic Partnerships at Humanities New York, where he leads collaborations with cultural institutions, scholars, and community organizations statewide. He has facilitated numerous Community Conversations and public dialogues across New York on history, democracy, power, belonging, memory, and civic life, including conversations spanning the American Revolution to urgent contemporary questions. Previously HNY’s Director of Grant-Making, he curated initiatives such as
The History and American Imagination
.  A humanities practitioner focused on public dialogue, Murphy has held positions at the Leon Levy Center for Biography and the Gotham Center for New York City History and holds a Ph.D. in American History from the CUNY Graduate Center.

events.description:
Migration and music go hand in hand.
From Victrolas to tapes to TikTok, in clubs and record stores, through changing attitudes to immigration, people have used sound to express the trials and sorrows, hopes and humor of risking the journey to a new life.
Join us for an evening of discussion and archival music recordings as
David Goren
and
Maria Margaronis
explore how immigrants to America have used songs, skits and recorded messages from the founding of Ellis Island to the present to connect with home, to find their way, and to feel less alone.
Doors open at
6:30pm
, program begins at
7pm
.
Maria Margaronis
and
David Goren
have collaborated on ten BBC radio documentaries since 2017. Their first piece, “
America’s Ottoman Diaspora
,” drew inspiration from the Ellis Island National Immigration Museum and its oral history & discography projects. Other work by David and Maria, like “
The Black Cantor
,” reflects on the migrant experience and relationships between communities in a new home. David has also created
The Brooklyn Pirate Radio Sound Map
, an interactive website with sonic essays showing how pirate radio serves local West Indian neighborhoods.

events.title: Helen Tworkov on Buddhism in America Across Generations with Oneika Mays & Cyrus Dunham, with Jared Bland
events.description:
BPL Presents welcomes Helen Tworkov, the founder of
Tricycle: The Buddhist Review
and the author of
Lotus Girl: My Life at the Crossroads of Buddhism and America
. Moderated by Jared Bland and co-presented with
Tricycle: The Buddhist Review
.
In this ranging conversation, Tworkov and a group of writers and practitioners from different traditions and generations will gather together at Brooklyn Public Library for a lively and expansive conversation about the challenges and benefits of Buddhism in America today.
PARTICIPANTS
Helen Tworkov
is the founding editor of
Tricycle: The Buddhist Review
, the first independent Buddhist magazine, and the author of
Zen in America: Profiles of Five Teachers
. With Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, she is the co-author of
Turning Confusion into Clarity
,
In Love with the World
, and
A World of Difference
, forthcoming in February 2027. Her memoir,
Lotus Girl: My Life at the Crossroads of Buddhism and America
, was a
Library Journal
best book of the year and received a starred review in
Publisher’s Weekly
. She lives in New York City and Cape Breton, Nova Scotia.
Oneika Mays
is a yoga and meditation teacher rooted in Buddhist and yogic traditions. Her work lives at the intersection of carceral wellness and collective liberation. She spent over a decade at Rikers Island Correctional Facility, where she served as the first mindfulness coach and helped pilot and establish its wellness program. She leads retreats and speaks to groups nationally on the power and practice of love— specifically lovingkindness (metta) as a tool for transforming how we live and relate to one another. Her debut book,
Sit With Me: A No-BS Journey to Mindfulness and Meditation
(HarperOne, March 2026), explores that practice through the lens of her time at Rikers. Oneika believes no one should be left out of the conversation about what it means to get and stay well.
Photo credit Keith Bratcher
Cyrus Dunham
is a writer from New York City. His first book,
A Year Without a Name
(2019), was a finalist for the Lambda Literary Award. His work has appeared in
The New Yorker
,
Granta
,
4Columns
, and
The Intercept
, among many other publications and anthologies. He is a Dornsife Fellow in Nonfiction at USC, where he is writing a book about the relationship between Buddhism and trans life and politics in the West.
Jared Bland
is a writer, editor, and former publisher who lives in Toronto and Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia. His first novel,
The Harmony
, will be published in August 2027. He also writes the
Lower City
series of crime novels under the pen name Alex Spring.

events.title: CBH Talk | Forgotten History: The Brooklyn Theater Fire of 1876
events.category: adults, author talks, book discussion, BPL Presents, brooklyn history, Center fo
events.description:
On December 5, 1876, a fire broke out during a performance at the Brooklyn Theatre, then one of the city’s most prominent playhouses. Within half an hour, the theater was destroyed and nearly 300 people had perished, making the Brooklyn Theatre fire one of the deadliest disasters in New York City history.
Marking the 150th anniversary of the fire, authors
Arthur Scinta
and
Melanie Gall
come together at CBH to tell the story of that terrible night. Their two new books present two different perspectives. Scinta’s
Brooklyn Ashes
reconstructs the disaster and its aftermath drawing on extensive research that include materials from the Center for Brooklyn History’s collections. He recovers the experiences of those who were there, including his own relative and exposes Brooklyn's dark, Tammany Hall era political underbelly's responsibility for the disaster.
Gall’s
Fire Witch
approaches the tragedy through the theatrical world that surrounded it. Focusing on Kate Claxton, the famous Gilded Age actress who survived the catastrophe, Gall illuminates the performers, personalities, and culture of Gilded Age theater and Claxton’s life and career.
Together, the two authors explore a rapidly growing Brooklyn, its vibrant theater scene and the perilous conditions inside 19th-century playhouses, and the failures in fire safety that helped turn an evening’s entertainment into catastrophe. They also consider how the disaster was reported, remembered, and ultimately faded from public memory. Moderated by CBH chief historian
Dominique Jean-Louis.
In connection with the program and the 150th anniversary of the disaster, CBH is curating a special pop-up exhibit featuring materials from the Center’s collections that bring the Brooklyn Theatre and the events of December 5, 1876 to life. These items will be on display from December 1 through December 11.
Participants
Arthur L. Scinta
is the town historian and former mayor of Pelham, New York. He has decades of experience in historic preservation, law, public service, and real estate. After a successful legal career at one of New York’s largest law firms, Scinta founded a residential real estate firm. Drawing on his background in architecture and historic preservation, he is an active writer and frequent speaker on local New York history. He has also founded, worked for, provided pro bono legal services to, and is a current and past board member of several organizations dedicated to promoting history and architectural preservation, including the Pelham Preservation Society, the Westchester County Historical Society, the Hendrick Lott House Preservation Association, and the Historic House Trust of New York City. This is his first book.
Melanie Gall
is a writer, theater historian, and performer, whose solo career has spanned from Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall in New York City to Royal Albert Hall in London. Melanie is dedicated to highlighting forgotten stories from the past, both through her books and her theater work. She has written several plays that have been performed around the world including
The Ballad of Isobel Gunn, Forbidden Cabaret, Opera Mouse, Ingenue,
and
Stitch in Time: a Knitting Cabaret.
She has recorded several albums, including “lost” knitting songs from WWI and WWII, Hebrew and Ladino music, Piaf and Brel songs from the cabarets of France, and an album of original music celebrating the forgotten history of Canada. Melanie lives between Brooklyn, NY and Ottawa, Canada with her rescue sparrow, Colette and Prince Feathers, a temperamental parakeet.
Dominique Jean-Louis, Ph.D,
is the Chief Historian of the Center for Brooklyn History at the Brooklyn Public Library. Among the exhibitions she has curated are
The Battle of Brooklyn: Fought and Remembered
,
Trace/s: Family History Research and the Legacy of Slavery in Brooklyn
, and a pop-up exhibition,
Memories Matter
, in the Euclid Avenue subway station as a collaboration with the MTA's Vacant Unit Activation Program. Previously, she held the position of Associate Curator of History Exhibitions at the New York Historical. She received her Ph.D in US History from New York University, with her doctoral research focusing on race, ethnicity, and immigration in post-Civil Rights Era Brooklyn schools.

events.title: CBH Presents AIRWAY | Stories from the ER

events.description:
Every day, hundreds of patients pass through the Emergency Department at Brooklyn’s Maimonides Medical Center. Each arrives with a story. But what about the stories of the doctors who care for them?
Join CBH as we partner with
AIRWAY
,
the storytelling series that brings emergency physicians out from behind the hospital curtain to share deeply personal accounts of life in the ER. Part showcase, part window into the human side of medicine, this unusual stand-up evening features eight emergency medicine doctors who take turns at the microphone to recount experiences that have impacted them in ways large and small.
Founded at Maimonides by physicians
Dr. Mert Erogul,
Dr. Josh Schiller
and
Dr. Arlene Chung
, AIRWAY began a decade ago as a teaching tool for emergency medicine residents. After growing into a wider forum for hospital professionals, now AIRWAY brings its storytelling to the public.
The evening features emergency physicians from Maimonides and other New York City hospitals whose accounts illuminate the extraordinary human drama of the emergency room. These are Brooklyn stories of life-and-death decisions, unexpected connections, moments of vulnerability, and small encounters that leave lasting impressions. They remind us that behind every medical encounter are two human beings, and each has a story to tell.
Please note: Advance registrations is required for admission to this program.
About AIRWAY
AIRWAY
is an organization dedicated to helping doctors reflect and build community through storytelling. For over a decade, we have held events for emergency physicians in New York City and around the country, in small local venues and at national conferences.  Airway collects and showcases stories from doctors from around the world.

events.title: Layli Long Soldier Discusses We with Fred Moten
events.description:
In
We
,
Layli Long Soldier
examines what it means to be in community, to be in relation with family, nation, history, and language.
We
is the first-person plural, the pronoun of inclusion in English. It is also
Wé
, the Lakota word meaning “blood”—what is shared and what is shed.
In this ingenious and insightful arrangement of poems, lyric essays, and her own visual artworks presented in full color, Long Soldier creates unique spaces of collaboration, mentorship, and shared knowledge. The 184 X’s signed to a broken treaty, the fringes of a winged dress braided in honor of children lost to Indian boarding schools, and intricate Lakota star quilts become shapes and patterns that convey collective kinship, memory, and grievance. “From this day forward,” Long Soldier writes, “I declare
a war of language
.”
PARTICIPANTS
Layli Long Soldier
is an Oglala Lakota poet, educator, and visual artist known for her research-based work in documentary poetics that draws from community conversation. Long Soldier’s first book,
Whereas
(​​Graywolf Press, 2017), utilizes prose, longform narrative sequences and disclaimers to confront the wording and empty gesture of S.J. Res 14, a congressional resolution of apology to Native Americans, passed as part of the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2010. The poems in the first half of
Whereas
contain strings of hyphenated words, irregular spacing, and abrupt line breaks, which complicate the process of reading and demonstrate the limitations of language when addressing historical injustices. Her series of poems on the weather, titled
Day Poems
and
Night Poems
, commissioned by the Holt/Smithson Foundation, evolved into a large-scale outdoor art installation featured in the
Invisible Prairie
(2023) exhibition at Tinworks Art in Bozeman, MT.
Long Soldier contributed narration and poetry to the 2022 documentary film
Lakota Nation vs. United States
, directed by Jesse Short Bull and Laura Tomaselli. The documentary explores the Lakota people's fight to reclaim the Black Hills, which were taken from them by the United States in violation of treaties. For the film, she composed a long poem titled "135 Xs", which refers to the signatures of the 135 tribal elders on the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie with the United States government. Her poems have appeared in
Poetry Magazine, The New York Times, The American Poet, The American Reader, BOMB
and elsewhere. Long Soldier has received numerous awards, including the Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature (2021), the Michael Murphy Memorial Poetry Prize (2021), the PEN/Jean Stein Award (2018), the National Book Critics Circle Award (2018), a Whiting Award (2016). She was a recipient of the National Artist Fellowship from the Native Arts and Cultures Foundation (2015) and a Lannan Literary Fellowship for Poetry (2015). She holds an M.F.A. from Bard College and a B.F.A. from the Institute of American Indian Arts. Long Soldier is a mentor in the M.F.A. Creative Writing Program at the Institute of American Indian Arts and Endowed Chair of the M.F.A. Creative Writing Program at Texas State University.
Fred Moten
teaches at New York University. His recent projects include a poetry collection,
Perennial Fashion Presence Falling
(Wave Books, 2023), a record album,
Fred Moten/Brandon López/Gerald Cleaver
(Reading Group Records, 2022), and an essay collection,
All Incomplete
(Minor Compositions, 2021), written with his long-time co-worker Stefano Harney. He lives in New York City with his partner, Laura Harris, and their kids, Lorenzo and Julian.

events.title: Classical Interludes: American Patchwork Quartet
events.category: adults, BPL Presents, classical interludes, live music
events.description:
American Patchwork Quartet (APQ), led by multi-GRAMMY® award-winning guitarist/vocalist Clay Ross, binds timeless American folk songs with jazz sophistication, country twang, West African hypnotics, and East Asian ornamentation. APQ’s sound is a masterful confluence of tradition and innovation, transcending culture, politics, and ideology. Their debut was recently nominated for “Best Folk Album” at the 67th GRAMMY® Awards.
A southern-born roots music aficionado, Ross is also the founder of  the world-renowned Gullah group Ranky Tanky. In APQ, Ross intertwines with other Grammy-winning artists: Harini Raghavan, a Carnatic vocalist and violinist, Moto Fukushima, an internationally acclaimed Issei jazz bassist, and Rudy Royston, a renowned jazz drummer whose fibers were honed by African American church traditions.
APQ resonates as a potent symbol of unity in diversity. It stands testament to the notion that, from a collage of varied backgrounds, a coherent and beautiful whole can be fashioned. Mirroring America’s cultural mosaic, APQ stitches together a story that’s both intricate and resilient. The fabric of their music is genuine—it neither feigns tolerance nor presents an overly-embellished image of unity.
Instead, each carefully chosen piece dives deep into America’s patchwork soul and shares the joys, sorrows, and unwavering hope of a nation crafted by shared dreams and diverse histories. Far from being a haphazard collection of musical scraps, APQ is a deliberately designed homage to America’s past and a showcase of its dynamic present. It beckons listeners to meditate upon our shared identity and relish in the musical threads that bind us. Just as an intricately designed quilt becomes a cherished family heirloom, when the distinct patterns of APQ’s music align in perfect harmony, the result is both a blanket of warmth and a timeless treasure.
Artist Bios:
Clay Ross is a 2x Grammy Award-winning artist and the founder of the Billboard chart-topping band Ranky Tanky. A native of South Carolina, Ross moved to NYC in 2002 and has since collaborated with artists as diverse as Gregory Porter, Snarky Puppy, and Bobby McFerrin. Winning multiple grants through the U.S. State Department, he has toured worldwide as a Cultural Ambassador.
www.clayross.com
Rudy Royston, a Texas-born, Colorado-bred drummer and educator, is known for his dynamic percussion skills honed over three decades. His career, deeply influenced by the celebrated late trumpeter Ron Miles, has seen him explore various genres. Since obtaining a Masters in Music from Rutgers University and relocating to New Jersey in 2006, Royston has collaborated with jazz icons like Bill Frisell, Jason Moran, and Ravi Coltrane. His dedication to music propels him to continually expand his horizons.
www.rudyroyston.com
Harini (Rini) Raghavan, is one of New York’s great talents in Indian classical and film music. She is both a dynamic singer and expressive Carnatic violinist. Born in Chennai and trained in Indian Classical from a very young age, she moved to the United States to attend Berklee School of Music, graduating with a major in Electronic Production and Design. She has performed and recorded with Grammy winning artists such as A.R.Rahman and composed music for the trending Indian Netflix show ‘The Fame Game.”
https://www.rinimusic.com/
Moto Fukushima, bassist and Grammy-nominated co-leader of House of Waters, blends Western classical, traditional Japanese, and South American music into unique jazz compositions. A Berklee alumnus, he has worked with artists like Mike Stern and Dave Weckl. House of Waters' albums have topped iTunes charts, and Moto has earned accolades like the Sports Emmy and ASCAP Plus Award. Currently based in NYC, his talents continue to resonate globally.
https://www.motobass.com/

events.title: Elena Dudum Discusses They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful with Cherien Dabis
events.description:
BPL Presents welcomes Elena Dudum's “deeply felt memoir" (as the Whiting Award judges noted) that "defies social erasures of the diasporic Palestinian experience” while exploring Dudum’s evolving relationship to Palestine.
In her Palestinian Christian home in San Francisco, Elena Dudum was raised in a household ruled by her father’s lectures. He taught her everything: the story of her grandparents’ flight from their homeland, the history of her family’s orange groves, and the facts of the ongoing occupation of Palestine. Above all, he taught her not to forget. Soon his lessons consumed her childhood, and Elena found herself shrinking from an inheritance that felt both sacred and suffocating.
For years, she resisted it all until a family trip to Palestine shattered the abstraction of her homeland. Checkpoints, razed olive groves, soldiers—it was all plainly in front of her, as were the ghosts of her family’s past. What was once always just out of reach, now pressed against her body. Back in the United States, something in her quietly unraveled. She tried to outrun what she now knew by burying herself in elite institutions and the rising world of tech, where ambition was rewarded and history was inconvenient. Eventually, the inheritance she thought she could escape demanded reckoning.
Braiding rich personal narrative with archival fragments and cultural critique,
They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful
traces one woman’s journey as she returns—slowly, deliberately—to her father’s lessons, determined to claim them on her own terms.
Participants
Elena Dudum is a Palestinian American writer whose work has appeared in
The Atlantic
,
Time
,
Cosmopolitan
, and
Bon Appétit,
among others. In 2025, she was awarded the Whiting Nonfiction Grant for Works-in-Progress for early chapters in
They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful.
Her work has been supported by The de Groot Foundation, Tin House, the Sewanee Writers’ Conference, and Hedgebrook. Born in San Francisco, she now divides her time between New York and London.
They Told Me Back Home Would Be Beautiful
is her first book.
Cherien Dabis
is an Emmy-nominated filmmaker and actress who is widely recognized as a pioneer of Arab American storytelling. Her latest feature, All That’s Left of You, which she wrote, directed, produced, and stars in, world-premiered to critical acclaim at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival. The film has since won multiple top honors, including the Golden Gate Award and Audience Award for Best Narrative Feature at the San Francisco International Film Festival, the GIO Audience Award for Best International Feature at the Sydney Film Festival, and both Best Film and Best Screenplay at the Malaysia International Film Festival. It recently received an Independent Spirit Award nomination for Best International Film, and was shortlisted for International Film Feature in the 98th annual Academy Awards.
Dabis first broke through with her groundbreaking debut feature Amreeka, which premiered at the 2009 Sundance Film Festival before winning the coveted FIPRESCI International Critics Prize in the Director’s Fortnight at Cannes. She followed with her second feature, May in the Summer, which also marked her acting debut opposite Bill Pullman and Alia Shawkat. The film opened the 2013 Sundance Film Festival after earning the prestigious Sundance/NHK International Filmmaker Award. In television, Dabis has directed and executive produced acclaimed episodes of the Golden Globe-winning series Ramy and guest-starred in Netflix’s Gotham and Peabody Award-winning comedy Mo. In 2022, she earned an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Directing in a Comedy Series for the celebrated “Boy From 6B” episode of Hulu’s hit series Only Murders in the Building. She went on to direct standout episodes in seasons two and three, as well as episodes of Netflix’s Ozark. As an actress, Dabis can also be seen in Prime Video’s Fallout and Tarik Saleh’s Eagles of the Republic, which premiered in competition at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival.

events.title: CBH Talk | The N-Word: Elizabeth Pryor on Her Famous Father and the Word That Defines Them Both
events.category: adults, author talks, book discussion, BPL Presents, Center for Brooklyn History
events.description:
In
Something We Said: Richard Pryor, a Notorious Word, and Me
, historian
Elizabeth Stordeur Pryor
turns her scholarly eye toward an intensely personal subject: her father, legendary comedian Richard Pryor. The daughter of a white Jewish mother and a Black father famed for bringing the n-word into the mainstream of American comedy, Pryor has written a book that is part memoir, part cultural history, and a courageous work of self-discovery.
Pryor is joined in conversation by author and entrepreneur
Nina Lorez Collins
, who brings a remarkable parallel story of her own to the evening. Her mother was the pioneering Black filmmaker, writer, and playwright Kathleen Collins. Decades after her death, Nina brought her mother’s largely overlooked body of work out of the archive, helping to secure her place in American cultural history and introduce her work to a new generation.
Two daughters, each discovering, interpreting, and reckoning with the complicated story of a parent. Join them for a conversation that moves between rigorous scholarship and deeply personal inquiry, exploring the history and enduring power of the n-word, race in America, family legacy, and the search for identity in a world still profoundly shaped by the color of our skin.
Participants
Elizabeth Stordeur Pryor
is a professor of history at Smith College where she teaches courses on race, slavery, and her father, comedic legend Richard Pryor. She is the award-winning author of the article “The Etymology of [N-Word]: Resistance, Language, and the Politics of Freedom in the Antebellum North” and the 2016 book
Colored Travelers: Mobility and the Fight for Citizenship Before the Civil War
. Her viral TED talk on why it’s hard to talk about the n-word has been viewed more than two million times.
Nina Lorez Collins
is an entrepreneur, author, community leader, and consultant with a career background in book publishing that includes literary agenting, scouting, writing, and literary estate management. With a BA from Barnard and an MS from Columbia in Narrative Medicine, she’s published three books, hosted a podcast, managed a community & events business, and also consulted in the realm of end-of-life care and health communications. events.description:
In collaboration with the Brooklyn Public Library, FourOneOne presents
Black Poems
, the quintet led by vocalist, composer and educator Fay Victor. Drawing from writers who have served as deep inspirations for Victor throughout her life—Nikki Giovanni, Ntozake Shange, Thulani Davis, Sonya Sanchez, Langston Hughes, Audre Lorde and Jayne Cortez—
Black Poems
uses eight of their poems as source material for a tapestry-based score and suite. Victor will be joined by poet and vocalist LaTasha N. Nevada Diggs, pianist Angelica Sanchez, drummer Lesley Mok, and bassist and fellow singer Devon Gates for the first
Black Poems
performance since 2022. Join us for an inspired interweaving of the Black music and literary traditions, performed by both burgeoning and established forces within New York’s creative music community.
Over the past 25 years, vocalist, composer and educator Fay Victor has expanded the terrain of America’s Black vocal tradition through a kaleidoscopic career—enveloping her musical upbringings in Brooklyn, Trinidad and Tobago, and Amsterdam’s vibrant “New Dutch Swing” scene of the 1990s. Her singular “everything is everything” approach—from speech to scat, song to call-to-action and interrogations into who gets to make “new music compositions”—has won her a devoted audience over a dozen albums as bandleader. Victor is an electrifying live performer, whose voice can turn from crystalline to gritty within the same breadth. Cecil Taylor was once moved to approach her after a set and exclaim, “Betty Carter would have SHOT you!” From November 2026 through January 2027, her residency with FourOneOne foregrounds the creative histories central to her practice, with the help of collaborators and friends including Terry Jenoure, Lyndon Achee, Jessie Cox, LaTasha N. Nevada Diggs, Devon Gates, Angelica Sanchez, Lesley Mok, and more.
FourOneOne is a non-profit organization supporting historically aware and rooted performance practices across genres, enabling New York’s many audiences to engage with multiplicity and alternative approaches to time and space.

events.category: adults, author talks, BPL Presents, brooklyn history, Center for Brooklyn Histor
events.description:
What did New York City look like before Europeans forever changed the landscape, forests, wetlands, waterways, and wildlife? Ecologist
Eric W. Sanderson’s
first groundbreaking book,
Mannahatta,
transformed the way we see Manhattan, peeling back centuries to reveal the astonishing natural world that existed before colonization. Now his ambitious new book,
Before New York
, expands that vision to all five boroughs.
The culmination of 25 years of research,
Before New York
takes readers on a journey deep into the natural history of this city. Drawing on historical and ecological evidence, along with extraordinary maps and illustrations, Sanderson uncovers New York City’s early landscapes and ecosystems, shining a spotlight on the intricate relationships between land, water, plants, animals, and people that once flourished here.
Join him for an illustrated presentation and a conversation with
Sue Donoghue
, President and CEO of Brooklyn Botanic Garden and former New York City Parks Commissioner. Together, they'll explore what the city's ecological past can teach us about the present, and how recovering that history might help us imagine a more resilient, sustainable future.
Participants
Eric W. Sanderson
is an ecologist who sees nature through the city. He currently serves as the Vice President for Urban Conservation at the New York Botanical Garden, where he also directs the Center for Conservation and Restoration Ecology. Sanderson is the author of the bestselling book
Mannahatta:  A Natural History of New York City
(Abrams, 2009) and its five-borough sequel,
Before New York:  The Natural Geography of the City: An Atlas and Gazetteer
(Abrams, 2026).  He is also the author of
Terra Nova: The New World After Oil, Cars, and Suburbs
(Abrams, 2013), on the (un)sustainability of the American economic system and how it might be reimagined with nature in mind; and lead editor of
Prospects for Resilience:  Insights from New York City’s Jamaica Bay
(Island Press, 2016).  His work has been profiled in
The New Yorker, National Geographic
magazine, NPR, BBC, and
The New York Times
and his TED talk has more than 3 million views. He has published more than 65 papers and technical reports addressing problems in urban, wildlife, and landscape conservation, drawing on experiences from Mongolia to Tanzania to Patagonia to Brooklyn. Sanderson earned a Ph.D. in ecosystem and landscape ecology from the University of California, Davis, in 1998. Learn more about his work at urbanconservation.nybg.org.
Sue Donoghue
is a prominent leader of New York City’s parks and open green spaces. On September 1, 2026, she became the eighth President and CEO of Brooklyn Botanic Garden (BBG), a beloved 52-acre garden originally designed by the Olmsted Brothers and opened in 1911. Donoghue brings extensive policy and operational experience to the role. Following an early career in finance, she spent nearly two decades leading major civic, environmental, and infrastructure initiatives across New York City. Most recently, she served as Commissioner of the New York City Parks Department, where she managed 30,000 acres of parkland and led a team of 7,000 employees. Under her leadership, the department completed over 240 capital projects representing more than $750 million in investments, with a strong focus on climate resiliency and equitable public access for all New Yorkers. Her executive experience also includes an eight-year tenure as President of the Prospect Park Alliance and Administrator of Prospect Park. Donoghue first joined the public sector in 2007, serving as Senior Advisor and Assistant Commissioner at NYC Parks through 2013. During this period, she orchestrated the agency’s participation in PlaNYC—Mayor Bloomberg’s landmark sustainability agenda—and directed major citywide environmental initiatives, including MillionTreesNYC and urban restoration partnerships for Jamaica Bay.
